rows.title: Asian American and Pacific Islander Identities and Cultures
rows.heading: Student Learning Outcomes

groups.heading: Student Learning Outcomes
outcomes: Critical Thinking: Think critically in reading, writing, and/or speaking about topics relating to how various aspects of identity such as race, class, gender, sexuality, and immigration status shape Asian Americans and Pacific Islanders experiences and how Asian Americans and Pacific Islanders politicize(d) themselves through their cultural expressions, thereby identifying problems, theses, arguments, evidence and conclusions.

Communication: Write or speak about topics relating to the creation and evolution of Asian American and Pacific Islander identities and cultures, the socio-political contexts from which AAPI identities and cultures emerge, disappear, return, and reemerge, and the implications of AAPI cultural productions and practices on larger societal structures and imaginations, thereby addressing problems, formulating theses, making arguments, analyzing and weighing evidence, and deriving conclusions.

Personal Actions and Civil Responsibility: Demonstrate an ability to understand one's role in society, take responsibility for one's own actions, make ethical decisions in complex situations, and understand that one has the power and ability to make decisions that make a difference on a personal, professional and global level.
Global Awareness: Articulate similarities and contrasts among cultures, times, and environments, demonstrating an understanding of cultural pluralism.

objectives: Analyze and articulate common Ethnic Studies concepts and terms such as race and racism, racialization, ethnicity, equity, ethno-centrism, eurocentrism, white supremacy, self-determination, liberation, decolonization, sovereignty, imperialism, settler colonialism, and anti-racism in analyzing AAPI experience, cultural productions and cultural practices.

Apply theory and knowledge produced by AAPI communities to describe the histories, critical events, contributions, intellectual traditions, lived-experiences, and social struggles of Asian Americans and Pacific Islanders in the United States, emphasizing agency and group-affirmation.

Use the lens of anti-colonialism, anti-racism, and equity for Asian Americans and Pacific Islanders to critically analyze the creation and evolution of Asian American and Pacific Islander identities and cultures, the socio-political contexts from which AAPI identities and cultures emerge, disappear, return, and reemerge, and the implications of AAPI cultural productions and practices on larger societal structures and imaginations.

Critically analyze the intersection of race and racism as they relate to class, gender, sexuality, religion, national origin, immigration status, sovereignty, language, and/or age in Asian American and Pacific Islander creative expressions, cultures, and identities.

Critically analyze various forms of AAPI identities and cultures to review how struggle, resistance, racial and social justice, solidarity, and liberation, as experienced and enacted by Asian Americans and Pacific Islanders in popular culture, music, performance arts, visual culture, film, digital/internet cultures and transnational productions are relevant to current and structural issues facing AAPI communities such as in immigration, settler-colonialism, multiculturalism, education and language policies.
Recognize and evaluate the contributions of AAPIs in media and cultural production, acknowledging technical and stylistic characteristics, with emphasis upon issues of greater cultural concern.

Describe and actively engage with anti-racist and anti-colonial issues and the practices and movements in AAPI communities for a just and equitable society through the ways the student consumes, critiques, connects, and creates knowledge and (counter)culture.

outcomes: Critical Thinking: Think critically in reading, writing, and/or speaking about the aims, methods, types, and problems of philosophy and philosophical inquiry at an introductory level, with an emphasis on the history of Western philosophy up to the end of the Medieval period, thereby identifying problems, theses, arguments, evidence and conclusions.

Communication: Write or speak about the aims, methods, types, and problems of philosophy and philosophical inquiry at an introductory level, with an emphasis on the history of Western philosophy up to the end of the Medieval period, thereby addressing problems, formulating theses, making arguments, analyzing and weighing evidence, and deriving conclusions.
Self-awareness and Interpersonal Skills: Demonstrate an ability to analyze one's own beliefs/positions in the context of meaningful philosophical inquiry.

groups.heading: Student Learning Outcomes
outcomes: Pre-Socratic: Explain and analyze a Pre-Socratic philosophical argument and discuss aspects that are indicative of that era.
Medieval: Explain and analyze a Medieval philosophical argument and discuss aspects that are indicative of that era.
Pre-Socratic vs Medieval: Critically evaluate the relationship between a philosophical argument from the Pre-Socratic era and a related argument from the Medieval era

objectives: Describe the aims, methods, issues and problems associated with philosophy and philosophical activity from the pre-Socratic origins to the close of the Middle Ages.

Identify, define and/or describe the philosophical terminology or nomenclature commonly used to classify positions, methods/approaches associated with the history of Western philosophy from the pre-Socratic origins to the close of the Middle Ages.

Compare and/or explain/contrast basic concepts, principles and theories commonly meaningful to philosophical inquiry in the history of Western philosophy from the pre-Socratic origins to the close of the Middle Ages.

Critically evaluate the arguments related to philosophical activity in their historical context from the pre-Socratic origins through the Medieval period, such as the positions of Plato, Aristotle, and Aquinas.
Trace the theoretical and practical consequences of concepts, principles and theories in their historical context from the pre-Socratic origins to the close of the Middle Ages.
Critically evaluate their own beliefs in light of the positions of significant thinkers in early western philosophy.
